title: Can a CPA Represent You Before the IRS? Practice Rights
metaDescription: Can a CPA represent you before the IRS? Yes. CPAs hold unlimited representation rights under Circular 230 once authorized on IRS Form 2848 power of attorney.
h1: A CPA Can Represent a Taxpayer Before the IRS Under Circular 230
cardBlurb: A Certified Public Accountant holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS for audits, collections, and appeals once authorized on Form 2848.
introText:
A Certified Public Accountant (CPA) can represent a taxpayer before the [Internal Revenue Service (IRS)](https://www.irs.gov) on any administrative tax matter. Under federal regulations, a licensed CPA holds unlimited representation rights before the agency, meaning the professional may represent clients regardless of who prepared the underlying tax return.

Representation authority allows a CPA to advocate for a taxpayer during audits, negotiate payment and collection arrangements, and dispute proposed adjustments through administrative appeals. To exercise these rights on behalf of a specific taxpayer, the CPA must be formally authorized through IRS [Form 2848](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-2848).

Without that signed authorization, IRS employees cannot disclose confidential return information or negotiate with an accountant regarding a taxpayer's account.

sections.heading: What Circular 230 Authorizes a CPA to Do
sections.body:
A CPA who is not currently suspended or disbarred from IRS practice holds unlimited representation rights before the agency under [Circular 230](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/circular-230-tax-professionals). To qualify, the accountant must be duly licensed to practice as a CPA in any U.S. state, territory, possession, commonwealth, or the District of Columbia. Under the IRS rules outlined in the agency's guide to [tax return preparer credentials and qualifications](https://www.irs.gov/tax-professionals/understanding-tax-return-preparer-credentials-and-qualifications), this federal authority applies across all 50 states for IRS administrative proceedings.

The scope of unlimited representation rights matches the practice rights held by attorneys and Enrolled Agents. While each credential requires different professional licensing examinations and state or federal oversight, all three groups share identical practice authority before the IRS. A detailed comparison of these credentials appears in the guide on [Tax Attorney vs. CPA vs. Enrolled Agent](/compare/tax-attorney-vs-cpa-vs-enrolled-agent/). These professionals can represent a taxpayer on any tax issue, including audits, collection actions, and matters before the [IRS Independent Office of Appeals](https://www.irs.gov/appeals).

In contrast, uncredentialed tax preparers operate under severe restrictions before the IRS. An Annual Filing Season Program (AFSP) participant holds limited representation rights, which permit the preparer to represent only clients whose returns they personally prepared and signed. Furthermore, an AFSP participant can appear only before revenue agents, customer service representatives, or similar frontline staff, with no authority in collection disputes or appeals. Preparers who hold a Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) without a credential or AFSP completion have held no authority to represent clients before the IRS since January 1, 2016.

sections.heading: Form 2848 as the Official Authorization Mechanism
sections.body:
IRS Form 2848, officially titled "Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative," is the document that legally authorizes a CPA to represent a taxpayer before the IRS. Filing this form grants the designated representative authority to receive confidential tax return information and perform tax-related acts on behalf of the taxpayer. These authorized acts include signing agreements, filing consents, and executing waivers regarding tax liabilities.

Form 2848 is not a blanket authorization covering all past and future tax filings. The taxpayer must explicitly list the specific tax matters, the relevant federal tax form numbers, and the specific calendar years or tax periods covered by the power of attorney. The authorization also extends to Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) examinations when specified on the form. A representative who is not explicitly authorized for a specific tax period cannot receive information or take action on that period.

A CPA named on the form must complete Part II, the Declaration of Representative. In Part II, the accountant lists their professional designation as a CPA, identifies their licensing jurisdiction, and attests that they are currently authorized to practice. The CPA also provides their Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number, a unique nine-digit identification number assigned by the IRS to authorized representatives. The CAF number is distinct from a Social Security number, an Employer Identification Number, a PTIN, or an enrollment card number.

sections.heading: Differences Between Form 2848 and Form 8821
sections.body:
IRS Form 2848 authorizes full legal representation, whereas [Form 8821](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8821) grants only information access without advocacy rights. Known as the "Tax Information Authorization," Form 8821 permits a designated individual or organization to inspect or receive confidential tax transcripts and account records from the IRS. It does not authorize the designated recipient to advocate, negotiate, or speak on behalf of the taxpayer.

Taxpayers often use Form 8821 when a lender, third-party administrator, or financial advisor needs to verify tax records without managing IRS correspondence. Because Form 8821 does not grant representation power, an accountant authorized only under Form 8821 cannot represent the taxpayer during an audit interview or negotiate an installment agreement. If a taxpayer needs an accountant to challenge an IRS notice or negotiate a balance due, Form 2848 is required.

The eligible parties also differ between the two forms. While Form 8821 allows a taxpayer to designate any individual, corporation, or entity to receive records, Form 2848 restricts representation to individuals who satisfy IRS eligibility rules. Eligible representatives on Form 2848 include attorneys, CPAs, Enrolled Agents, Enrolled Actuaries, Enrolled Retirement Plan Agents, corporate officers, full-time employees, certain family members, qualifying unenrolled preparers for returns they signed, and qualifying students or law graduates in tax clinics.

sections.heading: Filing Channels for IRS Form 2848
sections.body:
Taxpayers and representatives can submit Form 2848 to the IRS through an online portal, by secure fax, or through regular mail. The fastest method is the [IRS online submission tool](https://www.irs.gov/submit2848), which allows both the taxpayer and the CPA to submit authorization documents electronically with digital signatures. Using the online system requires identity verification through the IRS portal before uploading completed documents.

Filers who choose paper transmission must send the completed form by fax or mail to an IRS processing center determined by the taxpayer's geographic location. The [Instructions for Form 2848](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i2848) divide the United States into regional processing sites, each with a designated fax number and mailing address. Sending the form to an incorrect regional office can delay processing and the recording of the authorization in the CAF database.

The IRS instructions for Form 2848 do not state any filing fee for submitting the authorization. Filers should ensure that all entries in Part I and the representative declaration in Part II are complete and legibly signed before submission. Incomplete entries, missing tax years, or missing representative signatures will cause the IRS to reject the submission without updating the representative database.

sections.heading: Representation Scope and Limitations for a Named CPA
sections.body:
Once the IRS processes Form 2848, the CPA can manage communications, attend conferences, and negotiate directly with IRS personnel on the authorized matters. The representative can inspect tax transcripts, defend deductions during an examination, submit responses to automated adjustment notices, and appeal audit findings to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. If tax debt resolution becomes necessary, the CPA can negotiate installment agreements or submit compromise settlement proposals.

However, Form 2848 representation is confined to administrative matters within the IRS. Authorization on Form 2848 does not grant standing to represent a taxpayer in federal court, such as the United States Tax Court. As discussed in the analysis of whether [an Enrolled Agent can represent a taxpayer in Tax Court](/guides/can-an-enrolled-agent-represent-you-in-tax-court/), court representation requires separate admission to the court bar under specialized judicial rules. Furthermore, while authorizations for CPAs remain active until revoked or replaced, authorizations for student practitioners in a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic (LITC) or Student Tax Clinic Program (STCP) automatically expire after 130 days.

This overview provides general information regarding IRS representation procedures and does not constitute legal or tax advice. Taxpayers facing an examination or collection action should review their specific facts with a qualified tax professional.

faqs.question: Can a CPA represent a client before the IRS?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Circular 230, a licensed Certified Public Accountant holds unlimited representation rights before the IRS. A CPA may represent a taxpayer on audits, payment issues, and administrative appeals regardless of who prepared the original return.

faqs.question: Does a taxpayer need to file Form 2848 for a CPA to speak with the IRS on their behalf?
faqs.answer: Yes. The IRS requires a signed Form 2848 to establish official power of attorney before disclosing confidential tax information or allowing a CPA to represent the taxpayer. Without this form, agency personnel cannot discuss account details or negotiate case outcomes with the accountant.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Form 2848 and Form 8821?
faqs.answer: Form 2848 grants full power of attorney, authorizing the representative to speak, negotiate, and execute agreements on the taxpayer's behalf. Form 8821 is strictly an information authorization that allows a designated party to inspect or receive tax records without the authority to represent the taxpayer.

faqs.question: What is a CAF number?
faqs.answer: A Centralized Authorization File (CAF) number is a unique nine-digit identification number assigned by the IRS to an authorized representative. The CAF number links the representative's professional profile to the specific taxpayer authorizations recorded in the IRS database.

faqs.question: Can Form 2848 be filed online?
faqs.answer: Yes. Taxpayers and representatives can submit Form 2848 electronically through the official IRS online submission tool at IRS.gov/Submit2848. The online platform supports electronic signatures and requires identity authentication prior to document upload.

faqs.question: Is there a fee to file Form 2848?
faqs.answer: No fee is stated in the official IRS instructions for filing Form 2848. The form can be submitted online, by fax, or by mail to the IRS without paying an agency processing charge.
